name: Non-incisional double eyelid (suture method)

card.summary: Buried-suture double eyelid surgery creates a crease with stitches instead of an incision; popular in Asia, with literature focused on crease loss and suture complications.
card.aka: Buried suture double eyelid, suture method, stitch double eyelid
card.note: Crease loss, reoperation and suture-related eye complications are documented.

quick.overview:
The suture method forms an upper-lid crease by passing buried stitches through the lid so that skin is tethered to deeper tissue, without a skin incision. It is described as very popular in Asia, especially China.

Studies are retrospective and focus on how long creases last and on complications. Surgeons contrast it with the incision method, which involves a skin cut.
quick.mechanism: Sutures are placed through the eyelid at one or more points (for example two-point or continuous techniques) and buried, creating an adhesion that forms the crease line.
quick.risks: Reports describe suture exposure causing corneal damage, sometimes initially misdiagnosed, crease loss from suture loosening and reoperation, and suture-related complications needing removal.

lead: Non-incisional (buried suture) double eyelid surgery creates an upper-lid crease by placing stitches through the lid rather than cutting skin. Surgical papers describe it as one of two alternative approaches, the other being the incision method, and as very popular in Asia, especially China.[1][2][3]

Because it implants suture thread, authors say foreign-material complications must be considered.[3] Recent literature examines crease loss, reoperation risk by age and fat removal, and eyebrow position changes.[6][7][8][9][10]
The studies located are retrospective cohorts and case series.

The appeal for people seeking a brighter, wider-looking eye is that the crease can be created in a short procedure, with less swelling and a quicker return to normal life than the incision approach, according to descriptions of the technique.[11][12] East Asian blepharoplasty as a whole is reported as the most common aesthetic procedure in Taiwan, South Korea and other parts of East Asia.[11]

paras: Variants in the literature include two-point buried suture,[10] continuous buried suture,[7] hidden non-incisional suture,[6] and orbicularis-levator-tarsus fixation suturing.[5] Two modified techniques were proposed to reduce complications specific to buried sutures.[3]

The HIROSHIMA Study, a high-volume retrospective observational study, used multivariate analysis to examine crease loss after hidden non-incisional suture surgery.[6] Other retrospective cohorts compared one-year outcomes in 788 cases between younger and older patients,[7] examined reoperation after upper eyelid fat removal over 4.5 years,[9] and analysed age-related reoperation risk from suture loosening.[10]

Retrospective cohorts suggest that the age of the patient, whether upper-lid fat was removed during surgery, and the specific suture technique each relate to how often reoperation is needed; the reports cited analyse crease loss and suture loosening as the main reasons for revision.[6][7][9][10]

A Japanese series of 210 upper lids described suture-related complications and compared removal techniques.[1] Chinese series report corneal injury and conjunctival complications from exposed sutures, with one 14-patient study describing misdiagnosis before correct identification.[2][4]
A 2026 report examined eyebrow position changes after double eyelid surgery in relation to preoperative compensatory brow elevation.[8]

Wikipedia notes that buried sutures can sometimes irritate the cornea.[11] The Japanese series of 210 upper lids from 116 patients was designed to identify the best techniques for removing sutures that had caused complications, and a Chinese retrospective study of 12 patients from 2016 to 2019 examined the causes, management and prevention of corneal injury and other eye damage from buried sutures.[1][2]

Double eyelid surgery creates a crease in an upper eyelid that naturally lacks one. The reported share of East Asian women with a natural crease ranges from about 41 percent in Koreans to roughly 70 to 83 percent in Chinese and Japanese populations, and the main goal is to make the eyes appear larger and more open and expressive.[11]

The buried-suture approach is chosen when the lid has little excess skin or fat to remove. In descriptions of the method, a thread is passed through the full thickness of the upper lid at the level of the upper tarsal margin so that the skin attaches to the underlying levator aponeurosis, which forms the fold.[11] A review of non-incisional techniques in Asian patients describes them as simple, noninvasive and efficient, and its authors favour a full-thickness single continuous method with fine nylon thread; they write that suitable patient selection and method choice give a natural-looking lid and reduce loss of the crease.[12]

Double eyelid surgery was first performed in 1896 by Dr. Kotaro Mikamo in Japan, in the period after the Meiji Restoration.[11] Western observers have sometimes read the operation as an attempt to Westernise the eyes; Mikamo recorded that most Japanese women already had double eyelids and described the single-lid look as monotonous and expressionless, which supporters take as evidence that his aim was to emphasise an existing feature.[11] Suture-based fold formation became the main alternative to incisional surgery as methods spread across East Asia, and the surgery now has a large literature from Japan, China and Korea.[11][1][2]

Wikipedia's summary of the two main approaches says the non-incisional method is less complex, has a shorter operating time, and is associated with quicker recovery and fewer complications, but tends to give a static crease that does not change with expression and may diminish over time, with possible corneal irritation from the sutures.[11] The incisional method removes skin, fat and muscle, can give a more dynamic and permanent crease and can address redundant tissue, but requires a longer operation and recovery, with a risk of lagophthalmos (incomplete lid closure) if too much tissue is removed.[11]

Surgeons also combine procedures, for example a subbrow blepharoplasty with double eyelid surgery for upper-eyelid rejuvenation in Asian women, which has a registered 30-person study, or an epicanthoplasty alongside the crease surgery.[11][13]

sections.h: How the suture method creates the crease
paras: In the non-incisional approach, thread is passed through the upper eyelid so that the skin is tethered to deeper structures at the line where the crease is intended. Reference descriptions say the sutures run through the layers of the lid near the upper edge of the tarsal plate and bond the subdermal tissue to the levator aponeurosis, so that the skin folds inward when the eye opens.[11] Surgeons then differ in how many points they use, whether the thread is buried or looped, and how deep the bite is, which is why the literature lists two-point, continuous and hidden variants.[5][6][7][10]

One review-style description by surgeons who favour a full-thickness single continuous method with fine nylon thread says the goal is a natural, pleasing crease with a lower likelihood of later crease loss, provided the patient and method are chosen appropriately.[12]

sections.h: Who the method tends to suit
paras: The suture method is generally described as suited to people with thin eyelid skin, little excess fat or skin, and a wish for a quick recovery, whereas those with thick, heavy lids or marked skin laxity are more often steered toward incisional methods that can remove tissue and give a more lasting fold.[11][12] Reference summaries note that, unlike Western blepharoplasty, which mainly removes redundant skin, the Asian double eyelid depends on fixing the fold, and poorly understood anatomy can lead to unsatisfactory results.[11]

Some cohorts bear on this question. A study of 788 cases compared one-year outcomes between younger and older patients having continuous buried suture surgery,[7] and a stratified analysis examined how age relates to reoperation from suture loosening in two-point buried suture surgery.[10] A 4.5-year cohort looked at whether removing upper eyelid fat changed the reoperation rate and stability.[9]

The crease is sometimes created alongside other upper-lid work such as epicanthoplasty,[11] and a registered study has tested adding subbrow blepharoplasty to double eyelid surgery for upper eyelid rejuvenation in Asian women.[13] A 2026 report examined how eyebrow position changes after double eyelid surgery, with attention to whether patients had been lifting their brows before surgery to compensate for a heavy or hooded lid.[8] This is relevant to the overall look because a lowered brow after surgery can alter how open the eyes appear.

Double eyelid surgery is one of the most commonly performed aesthetic procedures in several East Asian countries, including Taiwan and South Korea, according to reference summaries.[11] Its history is debated: some Western commentators have read it as an attempt to look Western, while Dr Mikamo, who performed the first operation in 1896, recorded that most Japanese women already had double eyelids and described the single lid as looking expressionless, a framing the reference summary presents as evidence that his aim was to enhance a feature already valued locally.[11]

Within looksmaxxing and beauty communities the procedure is discussed mainly as a way to make the eyes appear larger and more defined with a modest recovery period, and the suture version is often contrasted with incisional surgery on grounds of cost, downtime and reversibility.

Evidence is retrospective: complication series,[1][2][3][4] and recent cohort analyses of durability and reoperation.[6][7][9][10] No randomised comparison of suture and incision methods has been published.

timeline.event: Kotaro Mikamo performs the first double eyelid surgery in Japan.[11]
Two modified techniques proposed to reduce buried-suture complications.[3]
Japanese series on treating suture-related complications published.[1]
HIROSHIMA Study on crease loss and further cohort studies published.[6][7][9]
